plan.summary: Budget leans on the two checkouts with a real household purchase link plus explicit sustainability motivation — Pantrygood for scale and Hearthstone Goods for intent — with tests on meal-kit, bedding/bath and sustainable-footwear audiences to see whether household-adjacency or shared values converts; Swiftcart is out as a cleaning-product competitor despite the best reach in the set.

recommended.name: Pantrygood
recommended.tier_reason: The score treated this as a mid category match, but the notes describe exactly the buyer this brand needs: a values-driven household replenishment shopper who already responds to sustainability and clean-ingredient claims, buying a pantry/subscription basket that refill cleaners slot straight into.
recommended.rationale: Shoppers here just restocked an $86 organic pantry order and their notes say they are 'Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims' — a $35 refill kit is a small, on-message add-on to the same household restock.

evidence.quote: Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims

recommended.risk: Grocery subscribers may already buy an eco cleaner from the same pantry brand, so incrementality could be lower than the claim match suggests.

recommended.name: Hearthstone Goods
recommended.tier_reason: Computed fit penalised low reach and a loose category link, but this is the sharpest purchase connection in the set: shoppers buying non-toxic cookware for a new home need cleaners for that same kitchen, and the notes confirm sustainability motivation.
recommended.rationale: Notes say 'Sustainability-motivated kitchen buyers' with 'new-home life events' driving purchase, and the non_toxic subcategory means the plastic-free, non-harsh pitch is already the reason they bought — a $35 refill kit against a $198 basket is an easy add.

evidence.quote: Sustainability-motivated kitchen buyers. Gifting and new-home life events drive purchase

recommended.risk: Only 2.8M monthly impressions, so even a strong conversion rate delivers limited volume; gift purchasers are buying for someone else's kitchen, not their own.

test.name: Kitchenly
test.tier_reason: The score zeroed values because meal kits carry no sustainability tags, but the purchase moment is real: family and couples households buying a recurring food box are the heaviest kitchen-cleaning replenishers, and $35 is half a typical basket.
test.rationale: Notes describe 'Family and couples households' on subscription — steady kitchen cleanup demand and a proven habit of recurring household deliveries, which is what refill plans need.

evidence.quote: Family and couples households. Convenience-motivated but food-interested

test.risk: Audience is 'Convenience-motivated' and shows no sustainability signal, so the refill workflow and plastic-reduction pitch may not land; measure whether the eco angle or the convenience angle converts.

test.name: Cloudfoot
test.tier_reason: The brief explicitly asks to reach shoppers who already care about sustainability, and this audience self-selected into sustainable footwear; that is a value-level hypothesis worth measuring even though the category score is zero.
test.rationale: Notes describe 'Comfort + sustainability messaging' working on urban professionals with a near-even gender split, so the plastic-waste message reaches proven eco-claim responders at a price well under their $118 basket.

evidence.quote: Tech-adjacent urban professionals. Comfort + sustainability messaging

test.risk: The link is the shopper's values, not the purchase — nothing about buying shoes cues a cleaning restock, so click-to-conversion may be poor.

test.name: Northbed
test.tier_reason: Values scored zero, but the record shows a genuine home-project moment: bedding/bath buyers setting up or refreshing a home cross-sell into home categories, and the advertiser's own interests include home_textiles.
test.rationale: Notes report 'High cross-sell with home and wellness' among design-conscious buyers, so a bath/bedding refresh is a plausible trigger for restocking home care with a refill system.

evidence.quote: Design-conscious urban/suburban buyers. High cross-sell with home and wellness

test.risk: $164 considered textile purchases are infrequent and design-led; a $35 utilitarian cleaner may read as off-aesthetic, and 3.6M impressions limit learning speed.

launch_summary.summary: Most of the $10,000 goes to two checkouts with a real household link: Pantrygood at $4,250 for scale and Hearthstone Goods at $4,250 for buying intent. The remaining $1,500 tests three audiences — Kitchenly (meal kits), Northbed (bedding and bath) and Cloudfoot (sustainable footwear) — to learn whether household adjacency or shared sustainability values converts better.
